# Smallholder Precision Ag
## "Sell the decision, not the sensor. One node per village, not per farm. The farmer is the user — the buyer is downstream."

---

## 1. Diagnose: the ARPU gap is 100×, so nothing survives a port

Your existing business sells an **instrument to a decision-maker who owns the land, the machine, and the P&L**. In India, Kenya, and Vietnam those three things are held by three different people, and none of them is the farmer alone.

| | Core markets (NA/EU) | Smallholder markets |
|---|---|---|
| Farm size | 200–2,000 ha | 0.3–2 ha, often 2–4 non-contiguous plots |
| Annual farm net income | $150k–$1M+ | $400–$1,500 (household, often part-farm) |
| Willingness/ability to pay | $3–8/ha/yr SaaS + $15–40k hardware | **$5–15 per farmer per year, paid at harvest, in one lump** |
| Actuator that executes advice | VRT sprayer, autosteer, fertigation controller | Knapsack sprayer, a hired tractor, a hand, a pump switch |
| Decision-maker | Farm owner/agronomist | Farmer + dealer who extends credit + coop that buys the crop |
| Boundary data | Precise, owned, stable | Absent, disputed, leased annually, no cadastral certainty |

**The arithmetic that governs everything.** A 0.6 ha rice plot in the Mekong Delta grosses roughly $900–1,400/yr. A genuinely good advisory service moves that by 8–15% — call it

run.userPrompt:
In 2026, an agri-tech company that sells precision-farming sensor bundles to large farms in North America and Europe is entering India, Kenya, and Vietnam, where farms are small, fragmented, and often reached only through cooperatives or input dealers. Connectivity, hardware affordability, literacy demands, and the value farmers place on different data outputs differ fundamentally from the company's existing markets.

Design a product strategy for adapting a precision-agriculture platform to smallholder markets, covering hardware simplification, delivery partnerships, and which analytics features to prioritize or drop.
